newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Britain's Major arrives in Bangladesh on Asia tour.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major arrives in Bangladesh on Asia tour.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major arrived in Bangladesh on Friday night after a whirlwind tour of India that saw him mobbed in Calcutta and feted in Bangalore.
Major flew in for talks with Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and opposition leader Begum Khaleda Zia.
The visit is the second leg of a south Asian tour that will also take the British leader to Pakistan.

Major has been privately criticised at home by nervous members of parliament from his ruling Conservative Party for scheduling a week-long foreign trip at a crucial time in the run-up to a general election, now no more than four months away.
But Major, unfazed by an opposition Labour Party opinion poll lead of some 20 points, has rejected such criticism, saying he remains Britain's leader and his job is to boost trade.

His tour of India, billed as an attempt to build long-term links with a potential Asian economic powerhouse, bore immediate fruit with the unexpected announcement on Friday of a 60 million pound ($100.8 million) investment by British Telecommunications Plc in India's largest mobile phone operator.
While in Bangalore Major basked in plaudits from India's media, with one newspaper summing up his tour with the headline: "He came, he saw, he conquered."
He was mobbed by business people at a reception in Calcutta, where aides had to link arms and form a cordon around him to protect him from well-wishers and autograph-hunters.
But domestic politics were never far away on his last scheduled foreign trip before the general election.

News that the Conservatives had decided to call a by-election in an English parliamentary seat left vacant by the death of the Conservative member, despite the likelihood it will lose and the government slip into an overall minority in parliament, provoked immediate speculation about the general election date.
Major denied to reporters that he had given up hope of seeing out his full term, suggesting May 1 was still his preferred election date. The last possible date is May 22.
Aides sought to refocus the media'a attention on the successes of the trip, designed to open doors and forge long-term commercial links.

Major's visit to Bangladesh is seen as a one-day diplomatic interlude between his stay in India and the final part of his tour in Pakistan, where he will hold talks with government and opposition leaders as well as travel to the Khyber Pass, the legendary gateway to the subcontinent.
He will also address industrialists in Dhaka on Saturday and visit development projects in the country, the second largest recipient of British aid after India.
